metaTitle: Best Leaf Blowers for Gravel in 2026
metaDescription: Six leaf blowers for gravel drives and paths, compared by speed control, volume and weight so leaves lift without throwing stones everywhere.
expertTake: The WORX WG520 is the best gravel blower because its 110 MPH jet and 600 CFM volume lift leaves while leaving most stones in place. The GRASSTIGON corded 390 CFM model is the value pick for a short gravel path near an outlet. Skip a high-speed turbo blower for gravel work: a 250 MPH jet turns your drive into a spray of projectiles.
introParagraphs: Gravel is a hard surface for a blower because the thing you want to move, a leaf, weighs a fraction of the thing you want to leave alone. A jet that is too fast lifts the stones with the leaves and throws them at windows, cars and shins.

That reverses the usual shopping logic. Volume and control matter more than peak speed, a flat or wide nozzle helps, and the ability to run a low setting for most of the job is worth more than a turbo button. Eye protection is not optional.

products.name: WORX WG520 12 Amp corded turbine blower, 600 CFM, 110 MPH
products.description:
The WG520 gets the gravel balance right because it is a volume tool, not a speed tool. A 600 CFM turbine moving at only 110 MPH shifts a wide sheet of leaves with a stream that is gentle enough to leave most pea gravel in place. That is the opposite of the 250 MPH jets common on cordless models, which excel on wet pavement but turn a gravel drive into a hazard.

Its two-speed control gives you a low setting for gravel and a higher one for lawn and patio. Because it is corded, it never runs out partway down a long drive, and the continuous power is a real advantage over battery models that sag as the pack drains. The tradeoff is range: you need a heavy gauge extension cord and a path that does not snag it on stones.

Ownership is minimal. Keep the intake clear of grass and leaf scraps, check the cord for cuts from sharp stones before each use, and store it dry. A turbine blower has few wear parts, so expect many seasons of service. One practical habit is to start at the house end of the drive and work toward the road, so the leaves you move are always heading onto grass or a bed rather than into a ditch full of gravel you then have to rake back.
products.bestFor: Gravel drives and paths where you want leaves lifted and stones left behind.
pros: 600 CFM volume at a gentle 110 MPH
Corded power does not fade mid-job
Two speeds for gravel and lawn
cons: Cord limits reach on a long drive

products.name: MTKOALA 1200W brushless cordless blower, 700 CFM, 200 MPH
products.description:
MTKOALA offers three speed modes, which is the minimum for gravel work: a low setting for loose leaves, a mid for damp leaves and a turbo you should almost never use on stones. The 1200W brushless motor produces 700 CFM, which is plenty for a drive, and the claimed 160 minute runtime applies to the lowest mode.

The 200 MPH top speed is the risk factor. On a gravel surface it will throw stones, so stay on the lowest setting and use short sweeping passes. Compared with the WORX at 110 MPH, you get the freedom of a cordless tool but must exercise more restraint.

Treat the batteries as the wear item. Keep them indoors in winter, avoid draining to empty, and clear the intake of fine gravel dust, which scratches the fan blades over time. If the stones start to move, release the trigger and drop to the lowest mode instead of trying to out-sweep them; a second pass at low speed is faster than raking a scattered drive.
products.bestFor: Cordless users who will keep the dial on low for gravel.
pros: Three speed modes for stone control
No cord to snag on stones

products.name: TOLOOCC 735 CFM cordless blower, 6 speed modes, 2 x 5.4Ah
products.description:
TOLOOCC gives the finest speed stepping of any blower here, six modes, and gravel is exactly where that matters. You can find the lowest setting that moves leaves without disturbing stones, rather than choosing between too gentle and too aggressive. The 735 CFM figure is the highest among the cordless options in this guide.

Two 5.4Ah packs are larger than the typical 4.0Ah pairs, so runtime on the low settings should be generous. The listing also mentions light snow and dust, which fits a general yard blower rather than a specialist tool. Against the MTKOALA at three speeds, the TOLOOCC is friendlier to a careful user.

Because gravel dust is abrasive, clean the intake grille after each session and wipe the battery contacts. Store the packs at partial charge and do not leave them in a hot shed. With six steps it is worth learning which one just clears dry oak leaves on your own gravel, then noting it, because the right step is different for fine pea gravel and for crushed rock.
products.bestFor: Owners who want to dial in the exact setting for stones.
pros: Six speed settings for stone control
735 CFM is the top cordless volume here

products.name: GRASSTIGON 7-Amp corded blower, 390 CFM, 210 MPH, 4 lb
products.description:
GRASSTIGON is a small corded blower that weighs about 4 pounds and offers two speed modes. The 390 CFM and 210 MPH figures give it a narrow, fast jet, so use the low setting on gravel. At that weight it is easy to carry along a path, and the plug-in motor never fades.

It cannot match the volume of the WORX at 600 CFM, so a long gravel drive will take more passes. What it offers instead is portability and a low cost of entry, which suits a short path, a patio edge or a garden walk.

A 7 amp motor is modest, so use a proper extension cord and avoid long runs of thin wire. Inspect the plug and cord for stone cuts and keep the intake clear of leaf fragments. Because the cord drags along the stones as you move backward, loop it over your shoulder or run it along the edge of the drive to reduce abrasion.
products.bestFor: Short gravel paths near an outlet on a tight budget.
cons: 390 CFM means more passes on a drive
210 MPH on high can throw stones

products.name: JAGROM 20V cordless blower, 680 CFM, two 3.0Ah batteries
products.description:
JAGROM is a compact 20V handheld with a 680 CFM rating and two 3.0Ah packs, the smallest battery capacity among the cordless picks here. For a short gravel path or a small courtyard, the volume is useful and the weight is low.

The smaller packs matter on a long drive. Expect to swap batteries sooner than with the TOLOOCC's 5.4Ah pair, so plan to start with a full pair and keep a charger nearby. The listing does not describe speed settings, so check the product page before buying; a single-speed blower is a poor choice for gravel.

Care is basic: keep the packs indoors, charge after use and wipe grit off the nozzle. A tool that sits dusty in a shed will have contacts that corrode. Keep a spare pair charged if the drive is long, and take a break between packs so the motor and cells can cool.
products.bestFor: Small gravel areas and courtyards where weight matters.

products.name: WILD BADGER POWER 53cc gas backpack blower, 559 CFM, 174 MPH
products.description:
This backpack uses a 53cc two-stroke engine for 559 CFM at 174 MPH, which is a measured speed for gravel work. A gas engine means no runtime limit, so it suits a long gravel driveway where a cordless pack would run out. At 19.6 pounds it is a real load, but the backpack harness spreads it.

The throttle gives continuous speed control, and holding it at a fast idle gives the gentle flow gravel needs. Compared with the WORX corded unit, you gain range and lose quiet, and compared with the cordless models you gain endurance and lose convenience.

Expect two-stroke upkeep: premix fuel, a clean air filter, a spark plug check each season and a drained tank for winter. Gravel dust clogs filters, so clean the air filter more often than on a lawn. Because the machine runs on a harness, adjust the hip belt before the first pass so the weight rides on your hips; a slack belt puts the full 19.6 pounds on your shoulders by the end of the drive.
products.bestFor: Long gravel drives and large properties with no outlet.
pros: No runtime limit on a long drive

buyingCriteria.explanation: Stones start to move once air speed is high enough to lift them, and pea gravel goes first. The WORX at 110 MPH moves leaves but leaves most stones, while 200 MPH or higher on the MTKOALA or GRASSTIGON will scatter them. Pick a blower whose low setting is gentle, and ignore the turbo figure, since turbo on stones is how windows and shins get hit.

Two settings are a minimum and six, as on the TOLOOCC, is better. A variable trigger is best of all. The ability to find the lowest setting that lifts a leaf saves you from chasing gravel back onto the drive afterward.

A high-volume, low-speed stream moves leaves across gravel without disturbing stones. 600 CFM like the WORX or 700 CFM like the MTKOALA covers a wide path. A 390 CFM blower like the GRASSTIGON needs more passes.

A long gravel drive can take 20 to 30 minutes of continuous blowing. A pair of 3.0Ah packs on the JAGROM may not last, while two 5.4Ah packs on the TOLOOCC should. Corded and gas models remove the limit.

A flat or wide nozzle spreads the air and reduces stone throw. Wear safety glasses and keep the nozzle low, pointing away from windows and cars. Never blow gravel toward people or pets. Before you start, walk the drive and pick up any large stones or glass, which a blower will turn into a hazard at even moderate speed.

A gravel drive means walking and holding a blower for a long time. The 4 lb GRASSTIGON is easy to carry, while the 19.6 lb WILD BADGER is a backpack load. Match weight to the length of your drive. A blower that feels light for five minutes can feel heavy at twenty, especially when held low and angled across a wide surface.

Capacity of the pack. More Ah means a longer run at a given setting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stone control
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated how gently each blower can run, comparing the WORX's 110 MPH and the TOLOOCC's six speed settings against 200 MPH-plus turbo jets. A blower that cannot go low was marked down for gravel.

howWeEvaluated.title: Volume and coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared CFM from 390 on the GRASSTIGON to 735 on the TOLOOCC. Volume decides how many passes a drive takes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Runtime and power source
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet, we weighed pack sizes from 3.0Ah to 5.4Ah and counted corded and gas models as unlimited. A drive needs sustained power.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: The 4 lb GRASSTIGON and 19.6 lb WILD BADGER sit at the extremes. We matched carry method to session length.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at wear parts, fuel upkeep and the way gravel dust abrades fans and clogs filters. Parts support and brand history mattered.

rows: Gas runs until the tank is empty

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: The WORX and GRASSTIGON never run out and weigh little. Their range is limited by a cord that can snag on stones. They suit short to medium drives near an outlet.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The MTKOALA, TOLOOCC and JAGROM let you walk the full length of a drive. Runtime depends on pack size, and turbo drains it. They suit drives without a nearby outlet.

howToChoose.note: Pick corded for short drives with an outlet; pick cordless or gas for long drives.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A low-speed, high-volume stream and a wide nozzle. Pea gravel is small and light, so it lifts at lower speeds than crushed stone. Keep the nozzle low and angled along the surface.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WORX WG520 at 110 MPH is the safest for pea gravel, and the TOLOOCC on its lowest setting is the best cordless option. Avoid turbo on the MTKOALA.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You have a long drive, want fine control or own a lot of loose gravel. The TOLOOCC's large packs and the WILD BADGER's engine both save time.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your gravel is a small path. The GRASSTIGON or JAGROM covers it at a low tier.

maintenance.why: Gravel dust is abrasive and clogs filters and grilles. A clean intake protects the fan and motor.
Sharp stones cut cords on a gravel drive. A damaged cord is a shock risk.
Store at partial charge indoors. Heat and deep discharge shorten pack life.
Fresh premix, a clean air filter and a spark plug check keep the WILD BADGER starting. Gravel dust clogs filters faster.
Stone chips can crack plastic nozzles. A damaged nozzle changes air flow and stone throw.

faq.q: Can a leaf blower damage gravel?
faq.a: It will not damage it, but it can move it. Use a low setting and a wide nozzle, and rake stones back afterward. Never use turbo on gravel.
The corded GRASSTIGON sits at the lowest tier and the TOLOOCC and WORX in the middle. Gas is higher. Spend for control and runtime rather than turbo power.

faq.q: Is a corded or cordless blower better for gravel?
faq.a: Corded gives steady power and low weight but limited range. Cordless gives freedom but limited runtime. For long drives, cordless with large packs or gas is more practical.

faq.q: Why does higher speed make gravel worse?
faq.a: Stones lift once air speed is high enough, so a 250 MPH jet turns gravel into projectiles. A lower-speed, high-volume blower is safer.
Yes. Even on low settings, small stones can fly. Wear eye protection and keep the nozzle pointed away from people and glass.

faq.q: How long will the blower last on gravel?
faq.a: Abrasive dust wears fans and clogs filters faster. Clean the intake and inspect the nozzle regularly, and a blower will last several seasons.
